Beehive Destruction

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Hundreds of swarms of honeybees are being decimated every month as honey poaching escalates.

Unique Selling Point:
Deliberate beehive destruction and the theft of honey is escalating across South Africa. Brazen thieves are targeting commercial hives placed in remote locations, hacking the structures to pieces, making off with the honey and killing the bees in the process. Videos from beekeepers show the destruction and the aftermath after such an attack. But besides their own livelihoods, loss of income means loss of jobs for farm workers and then there is the impact it has on food production. Most orchards rely on beekeeps for pollination services. Without bees there are no avocados, macadamias, cherries, apples and so much more!

Summary:
On Tuesday 25 May (ironically International Honeybee Day), large-scale Beekeeper, Craig Campbell suffered a massive loss. 235 of his beehives were destroyed. It is part of an escalating trend across SA where brazen honey thieves simply hack the hives to pieces to get at the honey. In the process they destroy the brood and the swarm is killed, lost forever. Since then we know of 5 farmers who have suffered a similar loss, albeit on a smaller scale. The implications of this loss is far-reaching as it is not just the beekeepers that are suffering a loss, the large scale destruction of beehives is impacting food production all across the country.

Further information:
Craig Campbell is the Managing Director of Peel's Honey and the Chairman of the KZN Beekeepers Association. He has been a commercial bee farmer in the KZN Midlands for many years. But honey is simply a by-product for him. His main business is providing pollination services to farms and orchards across the country. He rents out his beehives to farms from Port Edward to Bethlehem in the Free State, and his bees are responsible for pollinating a range of crops, from cherries to eucalypts. So having lost 235 swarms of bees has impacted the entire pollination industry across the eastern part of SA.

But this is not an isolated incident... Large-scale honey theft and beehive destruction has been plaguing the industry for years, and is escalating rapidly. In the past week Mokgadi Mabela has also suffered loss. Mokgadi, a third-generation beekeeper, harvests and sells pure, raw honey from environmentally sustainable hives placed on farms and in rural communities across Gauteng, Mpumalanga and Limpopo. And she too, is no stranger to loss.

On 17 June, two separate attacks occurred - on in Hilton KZN where 40 hives were stolen from a secure location, and in Wellington a farmer lost more than 50 hives to vandalism and honey theft.

BEEHIVE DESTRUCTION SCRIPT 1
UPSOUND
So here is just a scene of the absolute devastation done by some vandals….
V/O
27 May 2021
This was the scene at Craig Campbell’s apiary site in the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands in May this year...
UPSOUND
Here are swarms upson swarms…. Totally destroyed...
Craig Campbell
Can you imagine now when you get to your site, and it’s just all this wax just lying on the floor, all the combs, all the brood combs, all the young bees that should have been hatching out, are all just squashed onto the ground. All the dead bees, just lying there and you’re walking on a carpet of bees, it’s just soul-destroying.
UPSOUND
It just carries on and on and on...
LINK
Computer
Almost overnight Campbell’s video went viral, eliciting emotional responses from all over the country… because the fact is that most beekeepers in South Africa have experienced this kind of devastation on some scale or another...
V/O
The magnitude of Campbell’s loss - 235 destroyed hives - has drawn attention to an issue that has been plaguing beekeepers across the country for many years…
UPSOUND
Last night the farmer noticed the fence was cut and 40-odd beehives were stolen.
V/O
Less than a month after Campbell’s business was hit, thieves struck again… this time near Pietermaritzburg.
UPSOUND
Every single one of these tyres had a beehive on it yesterday.
Matt Walker
I was surprised. I was absolutely flabbergasted that somebody was able and willing to do that.
V/O
In a matter of hours Commercial Beekeeper Matthew Walker lost 41 hives. The thieves arrived in the middle of the night, and simply loaded the boxes onto a bakkie.
Matt Walker
We found scattered equipment on the side of the road so they obviously hadn’t strapped everything on.
V/O
For Walker, who farms with about a thousand swarms of bees, this was a huge financial knock...
Matt Walker
40 hives, the replacement value is probably, you’re looking at about 84,000 -- R2,000 a hive.
V/O
The reason for the continued theft and vandalism… honey
Craig Cambell
There’s always a market for honey. They’re probably either selling on the side of the road, uh, but then we’ve got other unscrupulous people who come along and get them to get as much honey as they can and they’ll either bottle it or sell it themselves further on.


V/O
Honey is expensive to make and expensive to buy… which makes it attractive loot for criminals.
Matt Walker
You can get up to R3,000 worth of honey from a beehive in a season. Obviously it’s in a good area and a good season to produce that quantity...
V/O
And the demand for honey has grown since the outbreak of the pandemic, says Gauteng-based beekeeper and vice president of South African Bee Industry Organisation - Tumi Mobu.
Tumi Mobu
I struggled to keep up because people were making their own concoctions for the upper respiratory and they wanted that honey.
V/O
Mobu too was a victim of beehive vandalism a few years ago at one of her apiary sites in North West...
Tumi Mobu
One day I woke up to go and check, you know, to monitor the progress of production of honey. About 70 boxes were vandalised, they were actually burned, turned into ashes.
V/O
The incident had a devastating effect on her business, says Mobu.
Tumi Mobu
I could quantify it to over 350 000 that is gone. It’s gone and no one can replace it.
V/O
In the Midlands, Walker has also seen the impact of Covid on their industry.
Matt Walker
During hard lockdown last year we noticed some of our worst vandalism, stealing of honey which we believe people were using either to eat for themselves or sell, or they were using to ferment and make alcohol.
LINK
Kitchen
Honey can be used for many things and is often a kitchen staple… but it’s not cheap. Prices range widely depending on the source and quality, … and you can easily expect to pay around R100 or more for 500g.
Tumi Mobu
I always tell my customers that you pay premium price for a premium quality.
Matt Walker
A lot of people are under the impression that beekeeping is an easy way to make money -- it’s like liquid gold.
V/O
But in fact there’s a lot of work going on behind the scenes, says Campbell who has been working with bees for 30 years.
Craig Cambell
We as beekeepers are trying to make the bees’ life easier. So we, we’ve got to give them a food source, we’ve got to give them a source of water and then we give them a place to live.
V/O
Each swarm is housed in a box hive with 8 to 10 frames to accommodate the honeycomb. Campbell lines the frames with sheets of recycled beeswax.
Craig Cambell
It gives them a foundation to work on. And then they start drawing it out like this, so the cells are now being drawn out and that’s where they put the honey or in the brood nest they start laying the eggs and so on, or the queen starts laying the eggs. And then eventually when it’s drawn out properly, you’re getting a frame like this. And this is where the bees put the honey in.
V/O
Once the hive is ready, you need to entice a swarm to move in and then it takes about 18 months to build-up the colony for optimal honey production.
Craig Cambell
If you have a colony that’s sort of this big, it’s useless to everybody. So you’ve got to build them up till they’re, it’s a full box of bees. Like this, it’s no good to anybody.
1’06” – 1’12”
A full swarm, I don’t know who’s counted them but there are about 80 000 bees inside them.
V/O
But for commercial beekeepers the impact of theft and vandalism goes far beyond honey production.
Craig Campbell
It used to be all about honey, but as times have changed, uhm, and with climate change we’re finding more and more that’s, we’re going away from honey and we’re going into pollination of various crops.


LINK
Coffee
70 to 80% of the food we eat depends on bees for pollination…. No bees mean no avocados, apples, litchis, nuts, vegetables and even no coffee...
Craig Campbell
1’35” – 1’48”
Through habitat-loss, chemicals, all that kind of thing uhm the wild bee population isn’t what it used to be and with modern agriculture like it is we have to bring in extra bees to get maximum pollination.


V/O


And this is the main business of commercial beekeepers today. They rent out their hives through pollination contracts to enable crops to provide maximum yield.
Matt Walker
Pollination demand is increasing year on year and we steadily need to grow between 300 and 400 swarms of bees a year for the next 5 years to keep up with our current contracts. That’s without taking on another client. As more and more macadamias are planted and they come of age, more and more swarms of bees are needed.
Warren
Bees play a massive, massive role in our operation. Through the pollination season we’re gonna have over 200 hives in this farm.
V/O
Blueberry farmer Warren Haviside says they rely on beekeepers to ensure an export-quality crop.
Warren
Having a good pollination schedule and rotation of hives ensures a higher yield for the grower...
Matt Walker
On your blueberries you can double your tonnage, every hectare for every second swarm of bees that you put on.
V/o
Walker currently has 18 beehives in this blueberry orchard and he has to keep a close eye on them during the pollination period. Every 14 days the hives are rotated -- new strong colonies are brought in while the current working swarms take a break.
Matt Walker
There’s just not enough forage for them to stay in here longer. Because we’re in a closed net environment the bees can’t get out to find anything else. It’s like a human just eating lettuce for two weeks. You’re gonna start looking a bit sick after a while.
V/O
And because the bees are working so hard at pollinating the berries, they’re not producing any honey during this time.
LINK
Hives
Hives used for pollination are moved across the country depending on which crop is flowering at a particular time. So, the bees that pollinate the Avocados in KZN today will likely end up in the cherry orchards of the Free State in August/September...
Craig Campbell
When we move our bees we’ll load them up in the evening when it’s dark and they’re all sitting inside, and then we’ll take them to the farm, wherever, whichever farm it is. We’ll put them down before sunrise and within an hour they’re already working quite happily bringing in pollen and you can see them working…
V/O
So when it is reported that a farmer lost 235 hives, that means 235 fewer bee colonies that can be moved from farm to farm to pollinate crops -- a huge setback for an industry that adds about R16 billion to the South African economy.
Kim McCall
I’ve had my fair share of theft over the last four or five years -- enough that I have questioned carrying on with bees a lot.
V/O
Kim McCall has around 300 beehives on sites around Pietermaritzburg. Nothing, she says, stops the would-be thieves...
Kim McCall
Even though most of my hives are in 6-foot razor wire enclosures it just slows the guys down, you know...
Tumi


Most of the apiaries are not our farms. So you can’t even impose on, you don’t have control over security of that particular farm.
Claire: What are beekeepers in South Africa doing to protect their hives from vandalism?
What I have seen other beekeepers do is that build cages, cages around their boxes…Others they go to an extent of getting in a security company to come and guard their hives.


Craig Campbell
A few years ago, I actually had armed guards sleeping next to the hives on a 24 hour basis, for the two months that the bees were on that particular crop.
V/O
But all the additional costs of safeguarding hives or replacing vandalised equipment makes beekeeping a lot less viable.
Kim McCall
Until something is done about this it is a livelihood that’s, you know, not even an option anymore, which means my two guys … that’s their livelihood too.
V/O
As things stand at the moment, the outlook for South African beekeepers is bleak, which could have a far-reaching impact on all of us...
Tumi Mobu
You can eat honey today, but then you won’t have apples and mielies and, and other things, other crops, for next week.


Craig Campbell
The question now is do we do we carry on, do we pack up, do we just scale down? We have to do something, or else we pack up and you go hungry.







PROMO 1
11sec
Hundreds of beehives vandalised, honeycombs ripped out and a carpet of dead bees… this was the scene at a commercial apiary site in May this year. We investigate the impacts of ruthless honey theft.




PROMO 2
21 Sec
Across South Africa beehives are being targeted by relentless plunderers, causing thousands of rands of damage for beekeepers. But could their appetite for honey jeopardise the country’s food security?






PROMO 3
21 Sec
Decimated beehives, plundered for their honey…

UPSOUND Here are swarms totally destroyed

We investigate the ongoing trend of honey theft that is threatening the livelihood of beekeepers across the country.

We’ll put them down before sunrise and within an hour they’re already working quite happily bringing in pollen and you can see them working… V/O So when it is reported that a farmer lost 235 hives, that means 235 fewer bee colonies that can be moved from farm to farm to pollinate crops -- a huge setback for an industry that adds about R16 billion to the South African economy. Kim McCall I’ve had my fair share of theft over the last four or five years -- enough that I have questioned carrying on with bees a lot. V/O Kim McCall has around 300 beehives on sites around Pietermaritzburg. Nothing, she says, stops the would-be thieves... Kim McCall Even though most of my hives are in 6-foot razor wire enclosures it just slows the guys down, you know... Tumi Most of the apiaries are not our farms. So you can’t even impose on, you don’t have control over security of that particular farm. Claire: What are beekeepers in South Africa doing to protect their hives from vandalism? What I have seen other beekeepers do is that build cages, cages around their boxes…Others they go to an extent of getting in a security company to come and guard their hives. Craig Campbell A few years ago, I actually had armed guards sleeping next to the hives on a 24 hour basis, for the two months that the bees were on that particular crop. V/O But all the additional costs of safeguarding hives or replacing vandalised equipment makes beekeeping a lot less viable. Kim McCall Until something is done about this it is a livelihood that’s, you know, not even an option anymore, which means my two guys … that’s their livelihood too. V/O As things stand at the moment, the outlook for South African beekeepers is bleak, which could have a far-reaching impact on all of us... Tumi Mobu You can eat honey today, but then you won’t have apples and mielies and, and other things, other crops, for next week. Craig Campbell The question now is do we do we carry on, do we pack up, do we just scale down? We have to do something, or else we pack up and you go hungry. PROMO 1 11sec Hundreds of beehives vandalised, honeycombs ripped out and a carpet of dead bees… this was the scene at a commercial apiary site in May this year. We investigate the impacts of ruthless honey theft. PROMO 2 21 Sec Across South Africa beehives are being targeted by relentless plunderers, causing thousands of rands of damage for beekeepers. But could their appetite for honey jeopardise the country’s food security? PROMO 3 21 Sec Decimated beehives, plundered for their honey… UPSOUND Here are swarms totally destroyed We investigate the ongoing trend of honey theft that is threatening the livelihood of beekeepers across the country.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Hundreds of swarms of honeybees are being decimated every month as honey poaching escalates.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Deliberate beehive destruction and the theft of honey is escalating across South Africa. Brazen thieves are targeting commercial hives placed in remote locations, hacking the structures to pieces, making off with the honey and killing the bees in the process. Videos from beekeepers show the destruction and the aftermath after such an attack. But besides their own livelihoods, loss of income means loss of jobs for farm workers and then there is the impact it has on food production. Most orchards rely on beekeeps for pollination services. Without bees there are no avocados, macadamias, cherries, apples and so much more!
metadata.Summary: On Tuesday 25 May (ironically International Honeybee Day), large-scale Beekeeper, Craig Campbell suffered a massive loss. 235 of his beehives were destroyed. It is part of an escalating trend across SA where brazen honey thieves simply hack the hives to pieces to get at the honey. In the process they destroy the brood and the swarm is killed, lost forever. Since then we know of 5 farmers who have suffered a similar loss, albeit on a smaller scale. The implications of this loss is far-reaching as it is not just the beekeepers that are suffering a loss, the large scale destruction of beehives is impacting food production all across the country.
metadata.Further information: Craig Campbell is the Managing Director of Peel's Honey and the Chairman of the KZN Beekeepers Association. He has been a commercial bee farmer in the KZN Midlands for many years. But honey is simply a by-product for him. His main business is providing pollination services to farms and orchards across the country. He rents out his beehives to farms from Port Edward to Bethlehem in the Free State, and his bees are responsible for pollinating a range of crops, from cherries to eucalypts. So having lost 235 swarms of bees has impacted the entire pollination industry across the eastern part of SA. But this is not an isolated incident... Large-scale honey theft and beehive destruction has been plaguing the industry for years, and is escalating rapidly. In the past week Mokgadi Mabela has also suffered loss. Mokgadi, a third-generation beekeeper, harvests and sells pure, raw honey from environmentally sustainable hives placed on farms and in rural communities across Gauteng, Mpumalanga and Limpopo. And she too, is no stranger to loss. On 17 June, two separate attacks occurred - on in Hilton KZN where 40 hives were stolen from a secure location, and in Wellington a farmer lost more than 50 hives to vandalism and honey theft.
